stories.headline: Update: Trump Dismisses Concerns Over USS Abraham Lincoln Conditions; Acting Navy Secretary Orders Carrier Home
stories.summary:
President Trump on Friday dismissed mounting concerns about the welfare of sailors aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, saying the carrier's nearly nine-month deployment to the Middle East in support of operations against Iran was "not nearly long enough." The remarks drew swift condemnation from military families and lawmakers who have raised alarms about reported food shortages, broken plumbing, and crew members contemplating jumping overboard. At least one sailor has already gone overboard, prompting a Navy investigation.

Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao announced Friday that the Abraham Lincoln would be returning to the United States following the deployment, which has set a record for uninterrupted time at sea exceeding 240 days. The USS George Washington, departing from the Pacific, is en route to the Middle East to replace the Lincoln. A group of House Democrats sent a letter to Cao demanding answers about conditions aboard the ship.

Supporters of the administration argue the extended deployment reflects the operational demands of an ongoing conflict with Iran and that the Navy is managing a difficult but necessary mission. Critics, including veterans, military health experts, and lawmakers from both parties, contend the prolonged deployment has created a mental health crisis and that Trump's dismissive comments show disregard for service members.

The Lincoln's situation has become a flashpoint in the broader debate over the U.S.-Iran war, now in its sixth month. Comedian Bill Maher and other public figures condemned the reported conditions, while Trump credited the deployment with advances in the conflict.

stories.headline: Update: Morocco Intercepts Over 100 Migrants as Spain-Italy Row Over Ceuta Escalates
stories.summary:
Moroccan authorities on Saturday intercepted more than 111 migrants near the town of Fnideq, roughly three kilometers from the border with the Spanish exclave of Ceuta, deploying riot police, navy speedboats, army officers, and drones to prevent a feared second mass crossing. The action came after social media posts had called for a new mass attempt following a late-July crisis in which approximately 78,000 migrants reached Ceuta by sea, with the city's mayor reporting 100 deaths. Spanish authorities deployed more than 1,500 security officers and installed a metal fence and floating barrier at the breakwater.

The crisis has fractured European Union unity over border policy. Italy unilaterally suspended Schengen free-movement rules with Spain and introduced border checks on arrivals from Spanish territory, backed by Finland and Denmark. The Czech Republic called for Spain's Schengen membership to be temporarily suspended. Spain reacted angrily, with Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez arguing Ceuta is not part of the Schengen area, and Madrid introduced reciprocal border controls against Italy after Rome refused to stand down.

Italy's Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani on Saturday defended Rome's position, saying his country had acted out of concern over a potential new wave of arrivals, not as an attack on Spain. He urged Madrid to direct pressure toward Morocco rather than EU partners. The diplomatic rift represents one of the most serious strains within the Schengen framework in recent years.

The Ceuta migrant crisis has broad implications for EU migration policy and the future of open-border arrangements, arriving as the continent already faces pressure from multiple migration routes. The episode has intensified calls from right-leaning governments for stronger external border enforcement, while humanitarian groups have raised concerns about deaths during crossings and the treatment of migrants intercepted on both sides of the border.

stories.headline: Update: Luigi Mangione Pleads Guilty to Murdering UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson
stories.summary:
Luigi Mangione, 28, pleaded guilty Friday in a federal courtroom in New York to the December 2024 murder of UnitedHealthcare chief executive Brian Thompson, marking the first time Mangione admitted in court to the killing. Standing before Judge Margaret Garnett, Mangione described how he had researched Thompson's company, posed as an investor to obtain information about a UnitedHealthcare conference, used a 3D printer to manufacture a gun, and shot Thompson on a Manhattan street on the morning of December 4, 2024. He faces the possibility of life in prison.

Mangione's statement to the court attributed his actions to years of severe back pain and frustration with the health insurance industry. "After years of enduring severe pains from a broken back" and dealing with UnitedHealthcare, he told the court he targeted Thompson. Thompson's family members sat in the front row of the packed courtroom, at times visibly emotional. Mangione had entered the hearing amid reports of a possible plea deal, but prosecutors confirmed he simply changed his existing not-guilty plea to guilty without any formal deal.

The case generated an extraordinary wave of public attention following Mangione's arrest, with some online commentators expressing sympathy toward him as a symbol of frustration with the American healthcare system, even as others condemned the killing as premeditated murder. Thompson's death left behind a family and set off a national debate about healthcare industry practices and executive security.

Mangione still faces a separate state murder charge in New York, which carries the death penalty under New York law, in addition to the federal case. His sentencing date in the federal proceedings has not yet been announced.

stories.headline: Qatar Denies Holding Three Iranian Pilots Captured During Start of U.S.-Iran War
stories.summary:
Iran has publicly accused Qatar of holding three Iranian military pilots captive for six months after their fighter jets were shot down during a combat operation at a Qatari military base on March 2, 2026, the third day of the U.S.-Iran war. In a letter to the International Committee of the Red Cross, Iranian Brig. Gen. Mohammad Bagherzadeh identified the pilots as Javad Salehi, Abdul Majid Dashtian, and Imran Behroshian, and alleged they have been denied contact with their families in violation of international law. A fourth pilot, Majid Kazemi, was killed in the same operation and his remains were returned to Iran.

Qatar categorically denied the Iranian claims, calling them "misleading statements." Foreign affairs spokesperson Majed Mohammed Al Ansari acknowledged that contact had been made with the pilots "after they violated Qatari airspace" but said no response was received and that Qatar had conducted search and rescue operations. Al Ansari said Qatar had invited Iran to review the details of those operations and was still awaiting a response from Tehran.

The dispute adds a new diplomatic dimension to the six-month-old U.S.-Iran conflict, drawing in Qatar, which has simultaneously been serving as a key intermediary in mediation efforts between Washington and Tehran. Qatar has previously stated that mediation efforts are continuing but that no direct U.S.-Iran talks are planned.

The incident underscores the complex web of relationships in the Gulf region during the ongoing war, with Qatar hosting a major U.S. military base while also maintaining ties with Iran and serving as a diplomatic back-channel. The pilots' fate remains unresolved and could complicate Qatar's role as a neutral broker in ceasefire negotiations.

stories.headline: Trump Signs Memo Ordering Navy to Revert Aircraft Carriers to Steam Catapult Systems
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump signed a memorandum Thursday directing the Navy to switch fighter jet launch systems on aircraft carriers from electromagnetic catapults back to steam and hydraulic systems. The directive, titled "Rebuilding the United States Navy and America's Shipbuilding Industrial Base," instructs Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao to develop a plan for the transition. The memo would require the next Ford-class carrier, the Doris Miller, to be built with steam systems, with all subsequent ships following suit.

Trump has long criticized the electromagnetic catapult systems — known as EMALS — installed on Gerald R. Ford-class carriers, calling them "too complex" and arguing they have contributed to cost overruns and delays. Thursday's action fulfills a pledge Trump made nearly a decade ago. The directive notes that the Navy has experienced "shipbuilding setbacks stemming from overly complex designs," resulting in "cost growth, delays, and cancellations."

Critics argue the reversal would itself cost billions and effectively discard technology already paid for. Sen. Mark Kelly (D-AZ), a Navy veteran, test pilot, and aeronautical engineer, sharply rebuked the decision, saying Trump should "stick to what he knows best — ballrooms, bankruptcy, and bulls***" rather than dictating specific engineering choices to the military. The story is drawing bipartisan attention given the enormous projected cost of the switch.

The move is the latest in a series of Trump administration actions reshaping Pentagon policy and procurement. Supporters contend steam catapults are more reliable and proven technology, while opponents say abandoning EMALS would represent a costly step backward and undermine the Navy's modernization efforts.

stories.headline: DNC Formally Approves 2028 Presidential Primary Calendar, Keeping South Carolina First
stories.summary:
The Democratic National Committee has voted to finalize its 2028 presidential primary calendar, again placing South Carolina first in the nominating process. Under the approved schedule, South Carolina will hold its primary on January 22, 2028, followed by Nevada on February 1, New Hampshire on February 8, New Mexico on February 15, and Michigan after that. The decision continues the party's post-2022 realignment away from Iowa and the traditional New Hampshire first-in-the-nation status.

The new calendar is designed to amplify the voices of Black, Latino, and labor voters early in the selection process — constituencies party leaders view as central to the Democratic coalition. The move has been controversial, particularly in New Hampshire, where state law has historically required the state to hold the first primary, creating potential conflict with party rules.

The decision comes as the DNC is also grappling with a widely reported fundraising gap ahead of the 2026 midterms. Locking in a 2028 road map signals the party is focused on long-term structural rebuilding even as it faces near-term electoral challenges. The primary ordering reflects lessons Democrats drew from the 2020 and 2024 cycles, where early-state demographics were seen as not representative of the broader party base.

Republicans have argued that the DNC's repeated reshuffling of primary states reflects internal division and that sidelining New Hampshire and Iowa weakens the party's connection to working-class voters in key swing regions. Democrats counter that the new order better reflects the party's diverse national base and increases accountability to a broader electorate.

stories.headline: BBC Seeks to Subpoena Trump Family Members in $10 Billion Panorama Defamation Lawsuit
stories.summary:
The BBC has sought to subpoena three members of President Donald Trump's family — Donald Trump Jr., Ivanka Trump, and Jared Kushner — as part of its defense against Trump's $10 billion defamation lawsuit over a 2024 Panorama documentary. Court filings reveal that BBC legal representatives attempted in May to serve the subpoenas in person, but were turned away at a Secret Service checkpoint at the Kushner-Trump Florida residence and denied access at Trump Tower in New York.

The BBC's legal team argues that all three family members have "personal knowledge" of Trump's intentions when he delivered his speech ahead of the January 6, 2021, Capitol riot — the speech at the center of the lawsuit. The filing draws on evidence gathered by a congressional committee, noting that Trump Jr. and Ivanka Trump were present when their father revised the speech, and that Kushner drafted a statement for Trump that would have condemned violence.

BBC lawyers are asking the court to allow the subpoenas to be served by email and certified mail, given the failed in-person attempts. The broadcaster has apologized for an editing error in the Panorama episode that gave "the mistaken impression" Trump made a direct call for violent action, but denies the error meets the legal standard for defamation and has asked for the lawsuit to be dismissed.

The case, filed in Florida, represents an unusually high-stakes legal confrontation between a sitting U.S. president and one of the world's most prominent public broadcasters. Trump's legal team has not commented on the latest filing. The BBC press office also declined to comment.

stories.headline: Massive Wildfire Tears Through Belgium's Largest Nature Reserve, Evacuations Ordered
stories.summary:
Firefighters from across Europe battled a large wildfire consuming Belgium's High Fens nature reserve on Saturday, with local officials describing it as the country's worst blaze in recent history. The fire, burning since Friday, has destroyed roughly a third of the reserve and prompted the evacuation of two nearby villages, with authorities warning the flames could reach residential areas. Belgium activated the European Union's civil protection mechanism, prompting aerial support from Sweden, the Czech Republic, and the Netherlands.

Nicolas Yernaux, a spokesperson for the Wallonia regional government, said the fire remained out of control as of Saturday afternoon and that crews were deploying all available resources to protect homes. Firefighters have faced difficult conditions due to the park's boggy terrain, moorland, and forests, in some areas allowing heathland to burn because it was too inaccessible to fight directly.

The Belgian blaze is part of a broader pattern of wildfire activity across Europe this summer. Fires were also reported in Landes, France — where 650 residents evacuated — as well as in Croatia, Spain, and Serbia. The EU's Copernicus climate monitoring service confirmed that western Europe experienced its hottest June-to-July period on record, contributing to the elevated fire risk.

The crisis adds to pressure on European governments grappling with the consequences of extreme heat and drought. The situation in Belgium is still developing, with officials monitoring wind shifts that have complicated firefighting efforts.

stories.headline: Ukraine Strikes Russian Roscosmos Space Facility in Samara Region
stories.summary:
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced Friday that Ukraine conducted a strike on a production facility belonging to Russia's Roscosmos space agency in the Samara region, deep inside Russian territory. Ukraine used domestically produced Flamingo missiles in the attack, marking a continued escalation of long-range strikes on Russian military and defense-related infrastructure.

The strike on a facility tied to Russia's civilian and military space program represents a significant broadening of Ukraine's target set, reaching hundreds of miles into Russian territory. Ukraine has increasingly relied on domestically manufactured drones and missiles to conduct such strikes, reducing dependence on Western-supplied weapons for deep-strike operations.

Russia has not confirmed the strike or provided damage assessments. The attack underscores Ukraine's strategy of pressuring Russian military-industrial capacity and signaling its ability to reach sensitive strategic sites well beyond the front lines.

stories.headline: AI Companies Suspected of Buying and Destroying Secondhand Books at Scale to Train Models
stories.summary:
Independent booksellers across the world are reporting an unprecedented surge in bulk purchases of secondhand books, with single orders rivaling a typical week's worth of sales. The buyers are intermediary companies whose ultimate clients are believed to be artificial intelligence firms seeking physical books to digitize and use as training data for large language models.

The trend gained clearer context after court documents were unsealed last month revealing that Anthropic, the maker of the Claude AI chatbot, ran an internal project called "Project Panama" with the stated aim of destructively scanning books on an industrial scale — removing spines, scanning pages, and recycling the physical remains. A 2025 federal court ruling by Judge William Alsup found that using purchased books to train AI was "exceedingly transformative" and permissible under U.S. copyright law, effectively opening the door to the practice.

Anthropics said it does not acquire rare or antiquarian books through its programs, and that sourcing physical books for training is a widely used industry practice. Critics, including booksellers and authors, have raised concerns about the destruction of cultural artifacts and the lack of compensation to original authors, even if the practice is now legally sanctioned. The episode highlights unresolved tensions between the AI industry's appetite for training data and intellectual property rights.

stories.headline: Alaska Senate Democrat Peltola Rejects Kamala Harris Endorsement Amid Red-State Campaign
stories.summary:
Former Rep. Mary Peltola, the Democratic candidate in Alaska's U.S. Senate race, has publicly distanced herself from a fundraising endorsement sent by former Vice President Kamala Harris on her behalf. Harris sent the email through her Fight for the People PAC, urging donors to contribute to Peltola's campaign — with a portion of proceeds reportedly flowing back to Harris's own organization.

Peltola, who represents a state Harris lost by 13 percentage points in the 2024 presidential election, indicated the endorsement was unsolicited and moved quickly to separate herself from it. The episode illustrates the ongoing difficulty national Democratic figures pose for candidates in Republican-leaning states, where association with the party's 2024 presidential nominee remains a liability.

The story reflects a broader pattern of internal Democratic tension ahead of the midterms, as candidates in competitive states navigate between energizing the party base and appealing to independent and crossover voters. Republicans are expected to use Harris-linked endorsements as a campaign tool against Democrats in swing and red states.

stories.headline: South Korea Proposes Official Talks to End Korean War
stories.summary:
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung used Liberation Day ceremonies on Saturday to formally propose peace talks with North Korea aimed at officially ending the Korean War, which has remained technically active under a 1953 armistice. Lee called for a "multi-layered security system" to reduce tensions along the demilitarized zone and offered to discuss practical measures to halt North Korea's nuclear program.

Lee, who came to power after his predecessor Yoon Suk Yeol was impeached for attempting to declare martial law, has pursued a policy of engagement with Pyongyang and Beijing. He told the ceremony the two nations should "put down our intentions to threaten each other" and sit face-to-face for discussions on peaceful coexistence, while acknowledging that full denuclearization remains a long-term goal and a freeze on nuclear production a more realistic near-term objective.

North Korea has not yet responded to the overture. The proposal comes just days after Pyongyang fired a ballistic missile into the sea — its 11th suspected test this year — and North Korean state media made no mention of Lee's offer, instead covering Kim Jong Un's own Liberation Day commemorations. Pyongyang has previously rejected Lee's outreach, criticizing US-South Korean military cooperation agreements.

The initiative carries geopolitical weight as President Trump, the only Western leader to have met Kim Jong Un, has expressed renewed interest in engagement with the North Korean leader. Lee has indicated he would support a Trump-Kim deal to freeze nuclear production as a step toward denuclearization.

stories.headline: Record Heat Wave Sears Europe; Deadly Floods Hit Japan and Midwest
stories.summary:
A record-breaking heat wave driven in part by human-caused climate change is sweeping across Europe, with Belgium logging its highest temperature of the summer on Friday. Drought-stricken fields and fast-spreading wildfires have challenged firefighters across the continent; at least one person was killed in Croatia after an overnight blaze engulfed homes and vehicles, and fires also swept parts of the United Kingdom.

In Japan, record-breaking rainfall — roughly three months' worth in 12 hours — triggered severe flooding across multiple cities east of Tokyo, killing at least five people and stranding thousands who spent the night in airports and train stations. Stormwater submerged cars and railway tracks; authorities warned that more rain is forecast even as floodwaters began to recede.

In the United States, approximately 20 million Americans remain under flood watches in parts of Indiana, Illinois, and Ohio following six days of heavy rain, with multiple communities evacuated. Meanwhile, the National Weather Service warns dangerous heat will persist through the weekend across the Southern Plains and Lower Mississippi Valley, where humidity-adjusted temperatures could reach 115 degrees Fahrenheit.

Hawaii faces an additional threat: Tropical Storm Lala is expected to strengthen into a hurricane before reaching the Big Island this weekend. The National Hurricane Center has issued hurricane warnings; the storm could drop up to 25 inches of rain and bring the risk of mudslides and rip currents.

stories.headline: Kennedy Center Board Votes to Put Trump's Name on Facade, Defying Court Order
stories.summary:
The Kennedy Center's board of trustees voted Thursday to add the inscription "Restored and Renovated By President Donald J. Trump" to the institution's facade and rename the plaza outside "the President Donald J. Trump Plaza" — moves that appear designed to circumvent a federal court ruling that had blocked Trump's name from being added to the center's official title.

U.S. District Court Judge Christopher Cooper, appointed by President Obama, ruled in late May that the board had exceeded its authority when it unanimously voted in December to rename the center "The Donald J. Trump and The John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts," finding that congressional approval is required for an official name change. The board also voted Thursday to close most of the center for two years for renovations — another action Cooper had blocked.

Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-OH), who sits on the board and brought the original lawsuit challenging the name change, said the Thursday vote sought to "circumvent" Cooper's ruling. Her attorneys, Norm Eisen and Nathaniel Zelinsky, called the vote "a show of blatant disrespect to the courts" and said the defendants would face renewed legal challenge.

The episode sets up a fresh courtroom confrontation over the limits of executive and institutional authority versus judicial orders. Supporters of the renovation argue Trump's substantial personal and political investment in the center's overhaul warrants formal recognition; critics contend the board is acting in defiance of clear judicial direction.

stories.headline: DNC Chair Warns Party Faces Severe Fundraising Gap Ahead of Midterms
stories.summary:
Democratic National Committee Chairman Ken Martin told an executive committee meeting Friday that while the DNC has raised a record amount in the 198-year history of the organization, it still faces a dire financial disadvantage against Republicans heading into the November midterm elections. Martin urged allies to increase contributions in the final months before Election Day, warning that "we need more" despite the record haul.

The financial disparity is stark at the party-committee level: the DNC ended June with just $16.3 million cash on hand and more than $18 million in debt, compared to the Republican National Committee's $129 million. On the congressional side, the NRCC held nearly $93 million and the NRSC $56 million, while their Democratic counterparts — the DCCC with $73 million and DSCC with $41 million — trail but by narrower margins. President Trump's super PAC, MAGA Inc., separately holds a $400 million war chest, though it has not yet deployed significant spending.

Martin attributed the imbalance in part to Republican incumbency advantages, saying the White House has "auctioned off the federal government" and is "getting their war chest filled by every corporation under the sun" — a characterization Republicans reject, arguing their fundraising reflects broad grassroots and donor enthusiasm for Trump's agenda.

Individual Democratic Senate candidates are faring considerably better. Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-GA) had $42 million on hand at the end of June, dwarfing his Republican opponent's $2.2 million, and Democrats hold similar leads in other key Senate contests including North Carolina. Strategists on both sides say the candidate-level money may partially offset the national committee gap, though the overall environment favors Republicans.

stories.headline: Jason Arday, Ex-Cambridge Professor at Center of Plagiarism Row, Found Dead
stories.summary:
Jason Arday, 41, who resigned last week as a University of Cambridge professor of sociology of education amid plagiarism allegations, has been found dead at an address in Battersea, south London. Emergency services found a man unresponsive Friday afternoon; the Metropolitan Police said the death is being treated as unexpected but not suspicious.

Arday had denied plagiarism allegations, acknowledging errors in his work but attributing some to his autism. He had said the controversy — which erupted after academic Nathan Cofnas published claims of numerous instances of plagiarism — had caused 'an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack.' Arday's family said in a statement that 'the campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason,' describing him as a 'gentle man who always wanted to see the best in everyone.'

Arday became Cambridge's youngest-ever Black professor at 37 in 2023, a moment widely described as a milestone. Cambridge vice-chancellor Prof. Deborah Prentice called the news 'desperately saddening,' and UK Education Secretary Lucy Powell urged people to 'remember there are real people with loved ones involved.' The circumstances of his death have prompted renewed public debate about the conduct of academic and online scrutiny.

stories.headline: Phoenix Air Traffic Controller Averts Potential Disaster After Two American Airlines Jets Share Same Flight Number
stories.summary:
A Phoenix air traffic controller averted a potential mid-air collision early Friday after two American Airlines aircraft were mistakenly assigned the same flight number — American 2482 — and briefly shared the same airspace. Audio of the incident, posted by ATC.com, captured the controller distinguishing between 'American 2482 on the arrival' and 'American 2482 on the departure' to prevent dangerous confusion over altitude directives.

The duplication occurred because a Chicago-bound flight was delayed by weather, prompting American to dispatch a second plane from Phoenix on the same route. With both aircraft aloft simultaneously, a dispatcher failure to catch the overlap in flight planning meant both pilots were operating under the same call sign. Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo, who has four decades of airline experience, said such incidents are extremely rare and praised the system's built-in redundancy.

The Federal Aviation Administration and American Airlines both confirmed they will investigate how the error occurred. The controller, who said he had never seen two aircraft 'pretty much merge with the same call sign' in 25 years, was complimented by one of the pilots for his 'nice work.' The incident comes amid ongoing national scrutiny of air traffic control staffing and aviation safety procedures.

stories.headline: Abbott Directs Grant Review Over DFW Airport Islamic Washing Facilities; Airport Drops Plan
stories.summary:
Texas Gov. Greg Abbott on Friday directed a review of state grants to entities operating Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport and George Bush Intercontinental Airport in Houston, citing religious accommodation concerns, and referred both airports to the U.S. Department of Transportation for investigation. The action came after DFW announced it would not proceed with a proposal to install Islamic ablution washing stations on the pre-security side of its international terminal.

Abbott wrote on X that 'government-owned airports cannot favor one religion over all others,' calling the DFW plan illegal. DFW said it had been evaluating the proposal and determined not to proceed after accelerated review, citing that the project 'would not deliver the originally anticipated operational benefits.' The airport had previously said details in a contractor filing — including a $300,000 cost estimate and a 'privately funded' designation — resulted from administrative errors by an outside design firm.

Supporters of the original plan argued that ablution facilities serve a broad international traveling public and that comparable amenities for other religious practices exist in airports globally, framing the accommodation as neutral customer service rather than religious favoritism. Critics, including Abbott, contend that installing faith-specific facilities at taxpayer-funded airports violates the constitutional principle of government neutrality toward religion. The episode reflects a broader national debate over religious accommodations in public spaces.

stories.headline: Builders Unearth €9 Million Gold Stash Hidden in Walls of Belgian Property
stories.summary:
Construction workers renovating a property in East Flanders, Belgium, discovered a trove of gold bars and coins estimated at €9 million sealed inside the cellar walls earlier this week. The find, made while drilling for new sewage pipes, is believed to be one of the largest such discoveries in recent Belgian history.

The property belongs to CAW Oost-Vlaanderen, a welfare charity in Dendermonde. Its director said he hopes the gold might eventually support the charity's work. Police have secured the hoard and warned the public against visiting the site. Under Belgian law, a rightful owner has five years to come forward; if no claim is established, proceeds are divided between the finder and the property owner — provided the stash is not linked to criminal activity.

Local prosecutors have launched an investigation into the origin of the gold. The incident has drawn international attention and raised legal questions about treasure ownership under Belgian civil law.
